extraction.name: Visual Question Answering Datasets
extraction.description: A comprehensive review of Visual Question Answering (VQA) datasets including DAQUAR, COCO-QA, The VQA Dataset (COCO-VQA and SYNTH-VQA), FM-IQA, Visual7W, Visual Genome, and SHAPES. VQA is a computer vision task where a system is given a text-based question about an image and must infer the answer.
extraction.creator: Kushal Kafle and Christopher Kanan, Chester F. Carlson Center for Imaging Science, Rochester Institute of Technology
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Multiple VQA datasets were created using different collection methods. COCO-VQA used Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) workers to generate questions and answers. COCO-QA used an NLP algorithm to derive QA pairs from COCO image captions. Visual Genome used two modes: free-form questions and region-specific prompting. SYNTH-VQA used synthetic cartoon images with 50,000 scenes.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Software Collection, Web Scraping
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Images from Microsoft Common Objects in Context (COCO) dataset, NYU-DepthV2 Dataset, YFCC100M, and synthetic cartoon images. COCO consists of 328,000 images, 91 common object categories with over 2 million labeled instances, and an average of 5 captions per image.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For COCO-QA, longer sentences are broken into smaller chunks for ease of processing. For SYNTH-VQA, synthetic scenes are made from over 100 different objects, 30 different animal models, and 20 human cartoon models with deformable limbs and eight different facial expressions spanning different age, gender, and races.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: For COCO-VQA, three questions per image were collected with ten answers per question from independent annotators. For DAQUAR-consensus, an average of five human annotated ground truth answers per question were collected. Visual Genome used free-form and region-specific question prompting methods. Visual7W uses multiple-choice with four plausible answers collected by prompting annotators to answer without seeing the image.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: For COCO-VQA, inter-human agreement is about 83.3%. Inter-human agreement is especially poor for 'Why' questions, with over 59% of these questions having less than three annotators giving exactly the same answer. More than 13% of the 'yes/no' answers have both 'yes' and 'no' repeated by more than three annotators.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: COCO-VQA: 10 answers per question; DAQUAR-consensus: average of 5 answers per question; Visual Genome: varies
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Natural Language Processing (NLP) algorithm for COCO-QA, Edge Boxes for region proposals, ResNet for object classification, word2vec for similarity computation
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: SYNTH-VQA human models span different age, gender, and races to provide variation in appearance.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: VQA has potential applications as an aid to blind and visually impaired individuals, enabling them to get information about images both on the web and in the real world. It can also improve human-computer interaction as a natural way to query visual content and be used for image retrieval without using image meta-data or tags.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Multiple biases exist across VQA datasets. COCO-VQA has strong language biases where 'yes/no' answers span about 38% of all questions with almost 59% answered with 'yes'. Image-blind algorithms using only questions can achieve 49.6% accuracy on COCO-VQA. Questions are sensitive to phrasing. Natural image datasets tend to have more consistent context and biases. DAQUAR contains exclusively indoor scenes. COCO-QA has only four kinds of questions limited to what is described in COCO captions.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: DAQUAR is too small to successfully train and evaluate complex models, contains significant clutter and extreme lighting conditions, with humans achieving only 50.2% accuracy. COCO-QA has grammatical errors and unintelligible questions due to NLP algorithm flaws. COCO-VQA contains subjective opinion-seeking questions without single objective answers, with inter-human agreement of only 83.3%. FM-IQA requires human judges for evaluation making it impractical. Multiple-choice evaluation can be gamed by learning to exploit answer biases rather than reasoning about images.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, Testing, and Validation of VQA algorithms. Datasets are used for both open-ended and multiple-choice evaluation schemes. Applications include aiding blind and visually impaired individuals, improving human-computer interaction, and image retrieval.

name.evidence: Visual Question Answering: Datasets, Algorithms, and Future Challenges

description.evidence: Visual Question Answering (VQA) is a computer vision task where a system is given a text-based question about an image, and it must infer the answer.

creator.evidence: Kushal Kafle and Christopher Kanan, Chester F. Carlson Center for Imaging Science, Rochester Institute of Technology, Rochester, NY, 14623, USA

inLanguage.evidence: The dataset was originally collected in Chinese, but English translations have been made available.

rai:dataCollection.evidence: COCO-VQA consists of three questions per image, with ten answers per question. Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) workers were employed to generate questions for each image by being asked to 'Stump a smart robot,' and a separate pool of workers were hired to generate the answers to the questions. In COCO-QA, QA pairs are created for images using an Natural Language Processing (NLP) algorithm that derives them from the COCO image captions. Visual Genome has much greater answer diversity compared to other datasets... Two distinct modes of data collection were used to make the dataset. In the free-form method, annotators were free to ask any question about an image... The creators of Visual Genome combated this by also prompting workers to ask questions about specific image regions.

rai:dataCollectionType.evidence: Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) workers were employed to generate questions for each image... In COCO-QA, QA pairs are created for images using an Natural Language Processing (NLP) algorithm that derives them from the COCO image captions.

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: With exception of DAQUAR, all of the datasets include images from the Microsoft Common Objects in Context (COCO) dataset, which consists of 328,000 images, 91 common object categories with over 2 million labeled instances, and an average of 5 captions per image. Visual Genome and Visual7W use images from Flickr100M in addition to the COCO images. It consists of 6795 training and 5673 testing QA pairs based on images from the NYU-DepthV2 Dataset.

rai:dataCollectionTimeframe.evidence: Beginning in 2014, five major datasets for VQA have been publicly released.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: Longer sentences are broken into smaller chunks for ease of processing, but in many of these cases the algorithm does not cope well with the presence of clauses and grammatical variations in sentence formation. SYNTH-VQA consists of 50,000 synthetic scenes that depict cartoon images in different simulated scenarios. Scenes are made from over 100 different objects, 30 different animal models, and 20 human cartoon models. The human models are the same as those used in [41], and they contain deformable limbs and eight different facial expressions. The models also span different age, gender, and races to provide variation in appearance.

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: COCO-VQA consists of three questions per image, with ten answers per question. Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) workers were employed to generate questions for each image by being asked to 'Stump a smart robot,' and a separate pool of workers were hired to generate the answers to the questions... For DAQUAR-consensus, an average of five human annotated ground truth answers per question were collected... Visual7W uses a multiple-choice answer framework as the standard evaluation, with four possible answers being made available to an algorithm during evaluation. To make the task challenging, the multiple-choices consist of answers that are plausible for the given question. Plausible answers are collected by prompting annotators to answer the question without seeing the image.

rai:dataAnnotationPlatform.evidence: Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) workers were employed to generate questions for each image by being asked to 'Stump a smart robot,' and a separate pool of workers were hired to generate the answers to the questions.

rai:machineAnnotationTools.evidence: In COCO-QA, QA pairs are created for images using an Natural Language Processing (NLP) algorithm that derives them from the COCO image captions... In FDA, the authors proposed to only use the region proposals that have the objects mentioned in the question... The Focus Regions for VQA and Focused Dynamic Attention (FDA) models both used Edge Boxes to generate bounding box region proposals for images... During test, the labels are obtained by classifying each bounding box using ResNet. Subsequently, word2vec was used to compute the similarity between words in the question and the object labels assigned to each of the bounding boxes.

rai:personalSensitiveInformation.evidence: The models also span different age, gender, and races to provide variation in appearance.

rai:dataSocialImpact.evidence: There are many potential applications for VQA. The most immediate is as an aid to blind and visually impaired individuals, enabling them to get information about images both on the web and in the real world. For example, as a blind user scrolls through their social media feed, a captioning system can describe the image and then the user could use VQA to query the image to get more insight about the scene. More generally, VQA could be used to improve human-computer interaction as a natural way to query visual content. A VQA system can also be used for image retrieval, without using image meta-data or tags.

rai:dataBiases.evidence: Relatively simple image-blind algorithms have achieved 49.6% accuracy on COCO-VQA using the question alone. Several other practical issues also arise out of the dataset's biases. For example, 'yes/no' answers span about 38% of all questions, and almost 59% of them are answered with 'yes.'... Natural image datasets tend to have more consistent context and biases, e.g., a street scene is more likely to have picture of a dog than a zebra... Apart from the small size, DAQUAR contains exclusively indoor scenes, which constrains the variety of questions available... The other major shortcoming is that it only has four kinds of questions, and these are limited to the kinds of things described in COCO's captions.

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: While DAQUAR was a pioneering dataset for VQA, it is too small to successfully train and evaluate more complex models... The images tend to have significant clutter and in some cases extreme lighting conditions... This makes many questions difficult to answer, and even humans are only able to achieve 50.2% accuracy on the full dataset. The biggest shortcoming of COCO-QA is due to flaws in the NLP algorithm that was used to generate the QA pairs... This results in awkwardly phrased questions, with many containing grammatical errors, and others being completely unintelligible... The dataset also contains many subjective, opinion-seeking questions that do not have a single objective answer... These complications are reflected by inter-human agreement on this dataset, which is about 83%... This approach is impractical for most research groups and makes developing algorithms difficult... A major problem with multiple-choice evaluation is that the problem can be reduced to determining which of the answers is correct instead of actually answering the question.
